title: Nucla Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Nucla wells have a 108 ft median depth, with finished well costs commonly estimated at $11,400-$20,100.
h1: What Nucla Well Records Show Buyers
intro_html:
Buying land around Nucla means looking past the existence of a well permit. Colorado DWR records show 459 permitted wells within five miles, but only 175 are recorded as constructed, 178 report a total depth, and 29 report a pump yield. Those gaps matter when you are trying to price a new well or judge an existing one.

The local records point to mostly fractured-bedrock and unnamed aquifers, with a median well depth of 108 feet. Nearby Naturita, Redvale, and Norwood provide useful regional context, but a neighboring well is not a guarantee for your parcel. Ground conditions, well location, casing, grout, pump setting, and water rights all need to be checked separately.

sections.heading: Nucla well depth and the ground below
sections.html:
Nucla wells are often shallower than buyers expect, but the spread is wide. The median reported depth is 108 feet. The middle half runs from 22 to 223 feet, while the 90th percentile reaches 306 feet and the deepest record is 640 feet.

Depth records show 48% under 100 feet, 41% from 100 to 300 feet, 10% from 300 to 600 feet, and 1% at 600 feet or more. That mix is useful for a preliminary driller's bid, not a promise. Permits most often name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with Dakota and Dakota Sandstone also present. Fractured rock can change abruptly over a short distance, so nearby well depth is one of the best first checks before buying.

sections.heading: How much water a Nucla well may produce
sections.html:
Only 29 Nucla-area records report a pump yield, so the yield statistics are based on a small subset. Among those reports, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 7.0 to 12.0 gallons per minute.

The recorded mix is encouraging for ordinary household planning: 72% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, 17% report more than 15, and 10% report 1 to 5. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute. That does not eliminate low-yield risk on an untested lot. Ask for the well completion report, pump test information, storage capacity, and any history of shortages. An exempt household-use well is generally limited to 35 gallons per minute under Colorado rules, and water rights still control use.

sections.heading: Nucla water levels and what the records reveal
sections.html:
Static water-level information is limited around Nucla. Just 3 records report a static water level, producing a median depth to water of 50 feet and a middle half from 28 to 135 feet. That is not enough evidence to call a regional water-table trend upward or downward.

A static level is also different from the water level while pumping. A buyer should ask when the measurement was taken, whether the well had rested beforehand, and whether the number came from a completion report or a later inspection. The aquifer names and fractured-bedrock setting suggest that water conditions can vary locally. Test the actual well rather than relying on the median, especially for a larger home, livestock, or irrigation plan.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Nucla, and when
sections.html:
Permit activity is not evenly spread through the decades. The records show 3 permits in the 1960s, 36 in the 1970s, 19 in the 1980s, 85 in the 1990s, 30 in the 2000s, 58 in the 2010s, and 153 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. Many permits are for monitoring rather than household supply: the use mix is 60% monitoring, 29% domestic or household, 10% stock, and 1% irrigation.

The most active names in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), Gordon Smith And Company, and Smith Drilling C/O Gordon R. Smith. Those records identify past activity, not current availability or a recommendation. Confirm licensing, insurance, references, mobilization charges, and what the bid includes before hiring a driller.

sections.heading: What a new Nucla well may cost
sections.html:
For Nucla's mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, the supplied cost model uses $50 to $75 per foot. At the 108-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $5,400 to $8,100.

A finished system is more than the borehole. Including a pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, the estimated total at the median depth is $11,400 to $20,100. Treat that as a planning range, not a fixed quote. A deeper hole, difficult access, casing and grout requirements, water testing, rock, or a longer utility run can change the final bill. Have the driller separate drilling, casing, grout, development, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, and testing so competing bids can be compared honestly.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building near Nucla
sections.html:
Environmental review deserves attention here. Within about ten miles, the records map 13 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 122 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. These mapped features do not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to obtain a current water test and review the well location, groundwater flow, and past land use.

Low yield, dry holes, poor casing or grout, and pump problems are separate risks. Septic setbacks, replacement-area requirements, access for drilling equipment, and a suitable building site should be checked before closing. Colorado DWR permit conditions and local water-right requirements may limit household, stock, or irrigation use. Do not assume a permitted well supplies every planned use.

sections.heading: A practical plan for a Nucla lot
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's permit number and completion report, then compare nearby wells in Nucla and Naturita rather than relying on a countywide average. Look for reported depth, yield, static level, aquifer, casing, and well use. If records are incomplete, budget for an inspection, pump test, and laboratory water testing before removing contingencies.

For a vacant lot, have a driller evaluate access, likely well location, drilling depth, and the relationship between the well and proposed septic system. Confirm the permit path with Colorado DWR before construction. On an existing home, verify that the pump, pressure tank, electrical service, storage, and treatment equipment are included in the sale and working under demand. The strongest decision combines the paper record with an on-site inspection and a realistic finished-system budget.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Nucla, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Nucla is 108 feet. The middle half of reported depths runs from 22 to 223 feet. About 48% are under 100 feet, while the deepest record reaches 640 feet. Because many permits involve fractured-bedrock conditions, a nearby well helps with planning but cannot guarantee your lot's depth.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Nucla?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $75 per foot in mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 108-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $5,400 to $8,100. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $11,400 to $20,100. Deeper drilling or difficult access can increase the quote.

faq.q: How much water do Nucla wells produce?
faq.a: Only 29 records report pump yield, so the sample is limited. Those reported yields have a median of 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 7.0 to 12.0. Seventy-two percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 10% report 1 to 5. Test the actual well before relying on its capacity.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Nucla, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit alone. Within about ten miles, records map 13 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 122 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Those features do not prove contamination at your well. Order current laboratory testing and review nearby land use, mine history, well construction, and septic conditions.

faq.q: Are there many new well permits around Nucla?
faq.a: Permit activity is substantial in the recent records. The area shows 153 permits from the 2020s, compared with 58 in the 2010s and 85 in the 1990s. The newest permit year is 2025. However, 60% of the recorded use mix is monitoring, while 29% is domestic or household, so permit counts do not equal new homes.
